newsitem.title: UK: ATHLETICS-THUGWANE AIMING TO WIN CREDIBILITY BATTLE.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-THUGWANE AIMING TO WIN CREDIBILITY BATTLE.

text.p: Josia Thugwane's life story reads like the script for a Hollywood film.
The South African 1996 Olympic marathon gold medallist was abandoned by his parents shortly after his birth and brought up by his uncle and grandmother.
His guardians were unable to afford to send him to school and so as a young boy Thugwane earned a few Rand by minding cattle and picking potatoes until he was old enough to work in the mines.
While there he discovered he had a talent for running and quickly showed his ability.

At the age of 20 he narrowly missed out on qualifying for the 1992 Barcelona Olympics, South Africa's first appearance at the Games since 1960, after finishing fourth in that year's national championships.
Thugwane was not deterred and made no mistake four years later in 1996, winning the South African marathon title and booking his place at the centenary Olympics in Atlanta.
Once in Atlanta Thugwane made the gold his own, surging away from two rivals to become South Africa's first black Olympic champion.
That story alone attracted film producers with whom Thugwane is negotiating. But what has happened since could form the basis for a sequel.
South Africans saw him as the second most famous person in their country after Nelson Mandela but his taste of fame turned sour when local gangsters threatened himself and his family.

"They thought I had earned a lot of money when winning the Olympics but I had to explain to them that all I had got was the gold medal, nothing more," said Thugwane, speaking in London prior to his appearance in Sunday's London Marathon.

Thugwane moved his family from the Johannesburg township of Bethal, where he grew up in a shack without electricity or running water, to the middle class area of Middlebergh and a home with high fences and security cameras.

But crisis followed crisis and after being beaten up in a dispute with another motorist in January, an incident in which he lost several teeth, Thugwane decided it was time seek a change of environment if he was ever to reclaim his status as a top-class runner.
Since February he has been training hard in New Mexico, often running more than 200 kms a week.
He has come to the London Marathon to prove that his Olympic triumph was not a one-off achievement.
"Obviously I want to win but if I can't then I will be
happy with just breaking my personal record," Thugwane said.
His best time of two hours 11 minutes 0146 seconds is much slower than most other top runners in the world and he is only the 16th fastest man in the field for the 1997 London Marathon.
His coach, Jacques Malan, acknowledges that there is widespread expectation that he will fall short on Sunday. "So many people are sceptical of his performance that we want to prove them wrong."
Thugwane's participation in London has meant that the race will be broadcast live on South African television for the first time.

With a $55,000 first prize and substantial time bonuses more than just pride is at stake. Thugwane could earn more in a few hours than he ever would have done in a lifetime in the South African mines.
But despite all his problems since the Olympics, Thugwane has at least been able to cash in on his celebrity status.
He has recently signed lucrative contracts with both Nike and Coca Cola. "We have a target of him earning around $600,000 for this year," said Malan. "Josia is well on the way to doing that."
